title: Delhi Just Banned New Petrol Two-Wheelers From 2028. No Indian State Has Gone This Far.
excerpt: The capital's new EV policy commits ₹15,000 crore, phases out petrol and CNG registrations for key vehicle categories, and plans 30,000 charging points by 2030.
body:
Delhi has drawn a line in the road. From April 1, 2028, not a single new petrol or CNG two-wheeler will be registered in the national capital. Only electric two-wheelers will be allowed. It is the most aggressive electric vehicle mandate any Indian state has ever imposed — and it took effect, in part, on July 1.

The Delhi Electric Vehicles Policy 2026, notified by the Lieutenant Governor on July 1, commits ₹15,000 crore (roughly $1.6 billion) over four years to rewire how the city moves. Chief Minister Rekha Gupta called it "a historic step toward effectively controlling vehicular pollution in the capital and promoting clean transportation."

The policy does not stop at two-wheelers. From January 1, 2027, only electric auto-rickshaws and small goods carriers will be eligible for new registration in Delhi. School operators must electrify at least 10 percent of their bus fleets within two years, rising to 30 percent by March 2030. Existing petrol and diesel vehicles are not affected — but the direction is unmistakable.

## The Incentives Are Substantial

To sweeten the transition, the government is offering purchase incentives through direct benefit transfer: up to ₹30,000 for electric two-wheelers in the first year, tapering to ₹10,000 by year three. Electric auto-rickshaws get up to ₹50,000, and small commercial trucks up to ₹1 lakh. All battery electric cars priced under ₹30 lakh receive a full exemption from road tax and registration fees.



> **"Chief Minister Rekha Gupta called it "a historic step toward effectively controlling vehicular pollution in the capital and promoting clean transportation."

The policy does not stop at two-wheelers."**


A scrappage programme adds another layer. Owners who scrap a BS-IV or older four-wheeler and buy an EV can claim up to ₹1 lakh. Two-wheeler scrappage brings ₹10,000, three-wheelers ₹25,000. Over ₹1,500 crore has been set aside for scrappage incentives alone.

Hybrid vehicles, notably, are excluded from every benefit. This is a pure-EV play.

## 30,000 Charging Points and a Pollution Crisis

The policy's most ambitious infrastructure promise: more than 30,000 public EV charging points across Delhi by 2030, funded through the central government's PM e-Drive Scheme and Delhi's own budget. Charging stations will be installed at markets, workplaces, and other high-footfall locations, with provisions for dedicated residential charging meters.

The urgency is real. Government data shows commercial goods vehicles account for about 33 percent of Delhi's vehicular pollution, while two-wheelers and three-wheelers contribute another 46 percent. A study published in *The Lancet Planetary Health* estimated that 3.8 million deaths in India between 2009 and 2019 were linked to air pollution. Delhi's PM 2.5 levels have regularly hit 300 micrograms per cubic meter — twenty times the WHO's recommended daily maximum.

Previous interventions — odd-even schemes, water trucks spraying mist, partial bans on fossil-fuel transport — have barely made a dent. This policy is betting that structural change will succeed where incremental fixes have failed.

## Not Without Skeptics

Industry observers have raised questions about execution. Puneet Gupta, a mobility analyst, noted that while the pollution case for EVs is strong, "charging infrastructure, supply chains, and China dependence remain key hurdles." India still imports the vast majority of its lithium-ion battery cells, and Delhi's power grid will need to absorb significantly more demand as tens of thousands of vehicles switch to electric.

The policy also excludes hybrid vehicles from all incentives, a decision that drew criticism from some automakers who argue that hybrids offer a practical bridge for consumers not yet ready to go fully electric.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs watching India's energy transition, Delhi's policy is a signal flare. The state is the country's political capital and a bellwether — when Delhi moves, other states tend to follow. Gujarat, Maharashtra, and Karnataka already have EV policies, but none have imposed outright registration bans on internal combustion vehicles.

The policy also deepens the investment case for Indian EV companies. Tata Motors, Mahindra, Ola Electric, and Ather Energy are all expanding capacity. For diaspora investors with exposure to Indian equities, the government's willingness to backstop the transition with ₹15,000 crore in public spending adds a layer of confidence that the market shift is not discretionary — it is mandatory.
